mishnayot.title: A flock that gets out of the pen
mishnayot.summary: An owner who shut his flock in properly is exempt if it still gets out. If he did not, he is liable. If the pen was broken at night or by bandits, he is not liable.

b: If he shut the flock in properly and it went out and caused damage: exempt. If not properly: liable.
If the pen was broken through at night, or bandits broke it, and the flock came out and caused damage: he is not liable. If the bandits brought out the flock, the bandits are liable.
The first mishnayot of the chapter review the laws of tooth and foot, and teach what kind of guarding frees the owner from them.
"Properly" means a door able to stand up to ordinary wind; that is enough for tooth and foot, which are attested dangers from the start.
The exemption for a break at night is for a break he could not have prevented; if the break was by day and enough time passed for him to find out and guard, he is liable.
If the bandits stood in front of the flock until it went out, it is as if they took it out by hand. If they only broke the pen, the damage is indirect (grama), and they are exempt.

mishnayot.title: The flock in the sun, and in a garden
mishnayot.summary: An owner is liable if he left the flock in the sun or gave it to someone who cannot be responsible. A flock that fell into a garden pays only what it benefited; one that entered normally pays for the damage.

outline.h: Left in the sun, or handed over
b: If he left the flock in the sun, or delivered it to a deaf-mute, a person with psychosis or a minor, and it came out and caused damage, he is liable. If he delivered it to a shepherd, the shepherd takes the place of the owner.
If he left the flock where the sun distressed it, it may break out of a properly locked door to escape the heat, so he is liable.
If the flock fell into a garden and benefited, he pays for the benefit. If it went down in its usual way and caused damage, he pays for the damage.
If it fell into the garden by accident, for instance down a slope from the public domain, and ate, it pays only what it benefited, as if it had eaten barley at the low price.
They assess what a se'ah's space of ground in that field was worth before and after.
Rabbi Shimon: if they ate fully grown produce, he repays in fully grown produce; one se'ah, one se'ah; two, two.
The mishnah's shepherd who "takes the place of the owner" is a shepherd who handed the flock to a second shepherd under him; the second takes his place. An owner handing a flock to a guard is in 4:9.
A se'ah's space is a field in which one sows a se'ah, 2,500 square cubits.

mishnayot.title: Sheaves stacked in a field
mishnayot.summary: The same rules as in 5:3, applied to a stack in another's field: without permission the field owner is not liable; with permission he is liable, if he accepted to guard.

b: If a man stacked his sheaves in his fellow's field without permission and the field owner's beast ate them: exempt. If the beast was injured by them: the owner of the stack is liable. If he made the stack with permission: the owner of the field is liable.

"The owner of the field is liable" means a guard of the threshing floors there, or a field owner who accepted to guard them. Rabbi (5:3) holds that letting someone in does not make him liable unless he accepted.

mishnayot.title: Fire
mishnayot.summary: The one who kindles a fire pays for everything it burns. The sages dispute how far the fire must spread. The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon: by the nature of the fire.

b: If a person sends fire in the hands of a deaf-mute, a person with psychosis or a minor, he is not liable by the laws of man but is by the laws of Heaven. If he sent it in the hands of a person of sound senses, that person is liable.
Kehati: a deaf-mute, person with psychosis or minor cannot be agents. An adult agent is liable, and the sender is exempt even from heavenly law, since there is no agent for a wrong act.
One brought the fire and another the wood: the one who brought the wood is liable. One brought the wood and another the fire: the one who brought the fire. Another fanned the flames: he is liable.
The last to cause the fire to spread is liable; the earlier contributors are exempt.
If the wind fanned the flame, they are all exempt.
This is only for an unusual wind. If it was an ordinary wind, the last is liable, since fire spreads in an ordinary wind and he should have guarded.
If it consumed wood, stones or dust: he is liable, for it says "stacked corn, standing corn, or the field" (Exodus 22:5).
If it passed over a fence four cubits high, or over a public way, or over a river: exempt.

A fire kindled in his own domain: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah: as if in the middle of a kor's space; Rabbi Eliezer: sixteen cubits, like a public road; Rabbi Akiva: fifty cubits; Rabbi Shimon: all by the nature of the fire.
The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon: if the fire is large, he is liable even beyond those distances.

mishnayot.title: What was in the stack
mishnayot.summary: A fire that burns a stack with utensils in it: Rabbi Judah says pay for all; the Sages, only for the grain. In a large building all agree he pays for everything in it.

b: If a man set fire to a stack and utensils in it caught fire: Rabbi Judah says he pays for what was in it; the Sages say only for a stack of wheat or barley.
The Sages agree with Rabbi Judah that if he burned a large building, he pays for everything in it, since it is the custom to leave goods in houses.
The Sages: he pays only for what is visible, the stack of wheat or barley, not for utensils hidden in it.
If a kid was fastened to the stack and a slave stood near by and they were burnt: he is liable. If a slave was fastened to it and a kid stood near by and they were burnt: he is not liable.

mishnayot.title: Sparks, flax and the lamp
mishnayot.summary: A spark from a hammer: liable. A camel's flax that catches a shopkeeper's light: the camel's owner pays; if the lamp was outside the shop, the shopkeeper does. Rabbi Judah: not for a Hanukkah light.

b: If a spark flew out from under the hammer and caused damage, he is liable.
Kehati: it is like one who throws a stone or an arrow.
A camel laden with flax passed in the public domain and its flax entered a shop and caught fire from the shopkeeper's light: the owner of the camel is liable.
But if the shopkeeper left his light outside, the shopkeeper is liable.
If it was a Hanukkah light, the shopkeeper is not liable.
Rabbi Judah: he put the Hanukkah light outside with permission, since it is a mitzvah to place it outside the door of the house.
The halakha does not follow Rabbi Judah.
